item.title: Conformal Risk Certificates for Portfolio Optimization Under Uncertainty: A Gated Reinforcement-Learning Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.14699v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement-learning portfolio policies can optimize allocations from prices, covariances, and prior positions, yet they lack a calibrated, replayable mechanism for certifying that a proposed allocation respects a bounded risk envelope before execution. Regulators increasingly expect automated portfolio systems to provide exactly this kind of pre-trade audit trail, interpretable risk limit, and human-oversight mechanism. Gated Conformal Semantic Risk Control addresses this gap by separating return-seeking allocation from text-conditioned downside-risk verification. An instruction-tuned language model maps timestamped disclosures into schema-validated semantic risk states over macro, liquidity, earnings, and sector channels. These states induce correlated ellipsoidal factor-shock uncertainty sets whose conformal radii are calibrated by rolling finite-sample prediction over localized semantic nonconformity buckets. An asymmetric second-order cone gate then checks each raw PPO proposal against a certified worst-case semantic loss budget. The gate stays inactive for compliant proposals and intervenes only when that budget is exceeded. In walk-forward out-of-sample tests on nine liquid U.S. Select Sector SPDR ETFs, Raw PPO earns a 12.7% annual return while incurring a 4.05% semantic violation rate. Gated-CSRC removes all observed out-of-sample semantic limit breaches while retaining an 11.7% annual return. This 100-basis-point auditable safety premium is smaller than the yield loss imposed by unconditional hard projection, and exact McNemar testing confirms the compliance gain at $p < 10^{-15}$. Loughran-McDonald lexicon controls and time-shuffled text controls fail to reproduce this certificate.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Zarei, Amirhossein MohammadpourAzari, Moslem Habibi

item.title: Idiosyncratic Market Effects in Global Time Series Momentum
item.description: arXiv:2611.15646v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Time series momentum is a pervasive explanatory factor in financial markets whereby a market's recent historical average return positively predicts future returns. Recent applications of statistical learning augment the traditional linear model definition with a more descriptive global nonlinear factor model. We extend the work of \citet{MoskowitzNonlinear} and demonstrate that models fit at the individual market level exhibit response curves that are distinct from the global factor model. We highlight the heterogeneity of forward market returns as a function of time series momentum and provide a framework that enables each feature-market pair to express its unique prediction behaviour. Empirical results demonstrate that, despite substantially smaller sample sizes, fitting nonlinear models to individual markets is a robust and often overlooked modelling approach that can result in a marginal improvement in out-of-sample performance.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Butler, Maciej Zawadzki, Adam Butler

item.title: Global Seasonality Factor Investing
item.description: arXiv:2611.15657v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study seasonality as a factor for predicting risk-adjusted returns across global futures markets. We document five seasonality anomalies that, in aggregate, are pervasive across bond, commodity and equity markets. We demonstrate that each seasonality factor produces excess returns that are not reasonably explained by established global time series carry, momentum and skewness factors. We apply recent innovations in statistical learning and fit nonlinear seasonality models at the individual market level, thereby allowing each feature-market pair to express its unique seasonal prediction pattern. We discuss candidate economic rationales for the existence and persistence of each seasonality anomaly. Walk-forward out-of-sample testing demonstrates that fast-moving seasonal patterns, such as day-of-week and day-of-month, produce strong gross performance but with extremely high turnover, resulting in negative performance net of transaction costs. In contrast, slower-moving seasonal patterns, such as day-of-quarter, day-of-half-year and day-of-year, produce positive gross performance and, with the exception of day-of-quarter, positive net performance. An equal-weight ensemble of seasonality models produces an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio that is competitive with, and uncorrelated to, established global time series factor portfolios. Empirical results demonstrate that adding seasonality to a global factor portfolio increases the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio by approximately $30\%$ over the full evaluation period.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Butler, Adam Butler, Maciej Zawadzki

item.title: Dynamic Scenario-Based Portfolio Optimization for Multi-Asset ETFs
item.description: arXiv:2611.16540v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Portfolio outcomes may depend as much on trading restrictions as on how returns are modeled. We compared historical moving-window returns with conditional scenarios from ARMA--GARCH models and a Student-$t$ copula for 30 U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds. Matched mean--variance and conditional value-at-risk portfolios were evaluated under long-only and limited long--short bounds over 946 sessions. Historical portfolios had higher observed reward--risk ratios in most comparisons, but no paired difference remained significant after multiple-testing adjustment. Conditional scenarios did not consistently reduce realized downside risk. We distinguished changes in target weights from trades required to rebalance holdings after market movements. Relaxing the target-adjustment limit changed exposures, turnover, and some returns more than varying scenario count or seed in the examined tests. These findings suggest that assessments of conditional return inputs should consider portfolio constraints and trading requirements.
item.dc:creator: Abigail A. Mensah, Ali M. Jaffri, Nicholas Appiah W. Brent Lindquist, Svetlozar T. Rachev, Frank J. Fabozzi

item.title: Aproximaci\'on pr\'actica a los m\'etodos de selecci\'on de portafolios de inversi\'on
item.description: arXiv:2410.11070v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper explores the practical approach to portfolio selection methods for investments. The study delves into portfolio theory, discussing concepts such as expected return, variance, asset correlation, and opportunity sets. It also presents the efficient frontier and its application in the Markowitz model, which employs mean-variance optimization techniques. An alternative approach based on the mean-semivariance model is introduced. This model accounts for the skewness and kurtosis of the asset return distribution, providing a more comprehensive view of risk and return. The study also addresses the practical implementation of these models, including the use of genetic algorithms to optimize portfolio selection. Additionally, transaction costs and integer constraints in portfolio optimization are considered, demonstrating the applicability of the Markowitz model. -- Este documento explorar la aproximaci\'on pr\'actica a los m\'etodos de selecci\'on de portafolios para inversiones. El estudio profundiza en la teor\'ia de los portafolios, discutiendo conceptos como el rendimiento esperado, la varianza, la correlaci\'on entre activos y los conjuntos de oportunidades. Tambi\'en presenta la frontera eficiente y su aplicaci\'on en el modelo de Markowitz, que utiliza t\'ecnicas de optimizaci\'on media-varianza. Se introduce un enfoque alternativo basado en el modelo media-semivarianza. Este modelo tiene en cuenta la asimetr\'ia y la curtosis de la distribuci\'on de retornos de los activos, proporcionando una visi\'on m\'as completa de riesgo y rendimiento. El estudio tambi\'en aborda la implementaci\'on pr\'actica de estos modelos, incluyendo el uso de algoritmos gen\'eticos para optimizar la selecci\'on de portafolios. Adem\'as, se consideran los costos de transacci\'on y las restricciones enteras en la optimizaci\'on del portafolio.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Minutti-Martinez

item.title: Mean--Variance Portfolio Selection by Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms, Regret Analysis, and Empirical Study
item.description: arXiv:2412.16175v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study continuous-time mean--variance portfolio selection in markets where stock prices are diffusion processes driven by observable factors that are also diffusion processes, yet the coefficients of these processes are unknown. Based on the recently developed reinforcement learning (RL) theory for diffusion processes, we present a general data-driven RL approach that learns the pre-committed investment strategy directly without attempting to learn or estimate the market coefficients. For multi-stock Black--Scholes markets without factors, we further devise an algorithm and prove its performance guarantee by deriving a sublinear regret bound in terms of the Sharpe ratio. We then carry out an extensive empirical study implementing this algorithm to compare its performance and trading characteristics, evaluated under a host of common metrics, with a large number of widely employed portfolio allocation strategies on S\&P 500 constituents. The results demonstrate that the proposed continuous-time RL strategy is consistently among the best, especially in a volatile bear market, and decisively outperforms the model-based continuous-time counterparts by significant margins.
item.dc:creator: Yilie Huang, Yanwei Jia, Xun Yu Zhou

item.title: Beyond Co-Movement: Locality by Exposures Enables a Joint Factor-Graph Framework for Portfolio Diversification
item.description: arXiv:2608.06618v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current portfolio construction methods are either agnostic to the effects of idiosyncratic shocks (standard factor models) or to the latent data structure driving systematic returns (recent graph-based approaches). This presents an opportunity to combine the complementary market aspects captured by the factor and graph domains, allowing asset allocations to operate directly on the underlying market structure, rather than on its observed co-movement or its finite-sample artefacts. In this work, we introduce the Mutually-INformed Graph-Locality and Exposures framework (MINGLE), which mutually regularises the factor and graph domains by redefining graph locality through systematic factor exposure profiles, rather than via observed co-movements. This is formalised through a unified Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) framework that jointly learns a latent factor representation and its induced graph topology directly from market returns. The resulting exposure-similarity graph aligns more closely with established economic sectors than conventional correlation-based graphs. Portfolios constructed from this representation are shown to consistently outperform their correlation-based counterparts across a range of volatility regimes and transaction cost levels. For rigour, paired statistical testing confirms that these gains stem from the reconciliation of the graph and factor domains.
item.dc:creator: Sara Chehab, Giorgos Iacovides, Parisa Yazdanparast, Danilo Mandic

item.title: Diffusion models for dynamic volatility surface generation and data-driven hedging
item.description: arXiv:2609.13402v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a diffusion-model framework for dynamic implied-volatility surface generation and evaluate its economic usefulness through data-driven hedging. The framework consists of two models. AD-Seq-Vol jointly learns the conditional evolution of the underlying asset return and the high-dimensional implied-volatility surface, generating adapted multi-period scenarios by sequentially updating the realized market history. AD-Seq-Vol-FT further incorporates option-market structure through post-training penalties for violations of static no-arbitrage conditions. Using daily SPX option data from 2000 to 2023, we show that the proposed models generate coherent surface trajectories while capturing both cross-sectional and temporal dependence. AD-Seq-Vol produces fewer and less severe static-arbitrage violations than the training data and the GAN-based benchmark, while AD-Seq-Vol-FT reduces these violations to nearly zero. We then integrate the generated conditional scenarios into an optimization-based hedging framework. Compared to a range of classical and data-driven benchmarks, the diffusion-based hedges maintain tracking errors near zero, substantially reduce tail risk, and exhibit particularly stable performance during the COVID-19 market disruption. These results establish Adaptive Sequential Diffusion Models as a promising class of market-consistent and economically useful financial scenario generators. Our code is available at: https://github.com/yinbinhan/volatility-surface-simulation.
item.dc:creator: Yinbin Han, Jack Yuxiang Zhang, Manuel Torres, Fernando Acero, Renyuan Xu
